new_statements.quote: p. 27: "The favoured syllable pattern of the word (free form) in Dravidian is (C)V̄CV/(C)VCCV/(C)VCVCV (three morae each). The other types are infrequent. There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Words can begin with vowels or consonants." p. 28: "Short vowels in non-root syllables (in unaccented position) tend to be lost." p. 26: "17. Pengo. Pop. 1,300. It is spoken in the Navrangpur district of Orissa. Burrow and Bhattacharya (1970) is the only source for Pengo."

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for Pengo, so this is the first statement held by the project: non-phonemic, initial-syllable loudness, family-wide. It is a family-level generalisation that includes Pengo, not a Pengo-specific description; the Pengo-specific ch. 2 pages (p. 56ff) were not read. The listed open_url (archive.org micro_IA41153650_0573) is a WRONG ITEM: a 1-page ERIC document resume (ED 475 049) for the book, not the book; archive.org advancedsearch finds no other item and Google Books search-inside (id 54fV7Lwu3fMC) could not be reached by automated download on three queries. The ch. 1 pages read come from an interlibrary-loan copy already held in the ling…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement covering Pengo (listed as language no. 17 of the family): stress is not phonemic in any Dravidian language; loudness normally falls on the initial syllable of the word regardless of its length, and a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels. Non-root (unaccented) short vowels tend to be lost.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not named as such; 'A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels' (p. 27) describes a weight-driven secondary prominence on non-initial long vowels.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the rule is hedged with 'Normally'. It is a typological generalisation over the family, not a Pengo-specific description.
new_statements.identity_note: Krishnamurti's statement is a typological generalisation over the whole Dravidian family (Pengo = no. 17 in his list, §1.4 p. 26: Navrangpur district, Orissa, ~1,300 speakers, Burrow & Bhattacharya 1970 the only source). It does not describe a particular Pengo dialect. The earlier reading notes two unpublished Osmania M.Phil. theses on the Avut and Indi-Awe dialects (Subba Rao 1982; Ramanaiah 1982); neither was listed here nor opened.
